items.title: 68002_Benny Waters oral history interview
items.q: even Charlie Parker when, he was one of the most progressive, Charlie eliminated many notes

ctx.x: to be a progressive type of musician?

Yeah, yeah, exactly. Now you can tell - I mean I kinda had proof of that. I tell you why now, wait a minute, I tell you why, I'm glad you brought that up. You remember I told you I's kind of mad about that deal too, when you was tellin' me, when I saw that 80 years old out there with nothing else - remember I told you? I said I don't play like some of the first New Orleans musicians my age, I play more modern, and you said yes, right? Well, that's it, that's the whole thing. Because otherwise I would be playing…

Let's turn the coin over. You cited that you're up in Boston, you're starting to be able to follow the world of jazz through records, which you weren't able to do earlier, primarily because there weren't records.

items.title: Benny Waters interviewed by Michael Woods, Los Angeles, California, September 1, 1995
items.q: I heard him in Kansas City with Jay McShann.

ctx.x: How did he change the way that alto sax players played?

Well Charlie gets credit for that see? Of pioneering in a new style. Firstly, I’ve heard Benny Carter play so much when he was young, see? And I always thought Benny was a pioneer also. He started at, particularly at that period. But I give Charlie the credit of changing the scene in alto playing. But you know he did most of that when he arrived in New York. I heard him in Kansas City with Jay McShann. He wasn’t playing exactly the same way. He was still, you could hear edges of his style coming out, but it…
If you, after all your many years of experience, if you could leave today’s music scene in our young and upcoming students —
